chapter: Early years with Paul Barnes and King Oliver
title: Nighthawks club in New Orleans, rejoining and leaving King Oliver
summary: Back in New Orleans Reason leads a Fats Waller-style small band, then returns to a ragged Oliver band in Savannah and slips away after a Vicksburg dance.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Oh yeah, I know him. Well, they had a band.

And the nighthawks on Roman and Kodai. And the club owner's name was Peter Tato, a tagging fella. And he had a color fella, was the manager named Peter Robinson from Mississippi. And I sat in with the band. During that time, Fetch Wilder's style was very popular. And I used to sing and play like him. And that first night I sat in with the band. And the manager called me on the side and asked me, I would like to work there. So I told him, Noah, he said, I'd like to make you the leader of the band. I said, well, I wouldn't want that. I said, I'll tell you, when you get rid of this band, then you call me and I'll choose my own man. See, they were playing more like on a big band style, which was different from Fetch Wilder's style. And I knew I had to train them. And I got, I hired Paul D. Barnes to play clarinet. I didn't want them to play sax, because Fetch Wilder's style then was clarinet and trumpet and chord rhythm, bass, piano, guitar and drums. And I worked there, oh, I guess about eight, seven, eight months. Then King Oliver sent for me to come back to the band, see if I could revamp the band. I went back to King Oliver's band. And I joined him in Savannah, Georgia. And we got on the road. And he had, it was just about the last round up then. He had a bunch of musicians. The band was a raggedy band. And not only musically, but clothes-wise too. I guess I had the only decency in the whole band. And I looked through the arrangements, and they were all messed up. And so I told King, I said, the only thing I can do, because I was an arranger then, I said, I'll have you just write you a whole new repertoire. So we continued to try and, try to revamp the band and doing a little bit of rehearsing. And we bought some orchestrations. And I saw where things had gotten so, so bad. And these fellas just didn't have it as being professional musicians. The name of King Oliver up. And we played a dance in Vicksburg, Mississippi. And when we played this dance, I met a woman. And I told her, I said, I'm going to leave this band. She said, well, when you going? Where you going? I said, I'm going back to New Orleans. I said, after this dance is over tonight, I'm coming by your house. I said, don't you tell anybody. And I'm not going to let King Oliver out talk me. And we played out in a place they call the park. And when I got finished, she had a little old call there. And I put my clothes in there and went on to her house. And I stayed there about two or three days. And after King Oliver, he had, he was a pretty wise fella. He knew just about what had happened. And I got free trained. Came and went back to New Orleans. Yes. And this day that I got into New Orleans, I went where Joe Robichaux was playing. Have you heard of Joe Robichaux?
